title: A mole in the White House? Residential proxies are everywhere
summary: Residential proxies are often used by bad actors to hide the true source of internet traffic — and now one of them appears to have taken up residence in the White House. The Residential Proxy Observatory , set up by Layer3 Intel to monitor the threat of anonymized network activity, has identified proxy exit activity on one particular network, AS2650, which is registered to the executive office of the US President and operated out of the White House. Residential proxies — so-called because they typically run on home or personal devices — mask the true source of internet traffic by rerouting it to appear to come from a different IP address. While it may be concerning that this is activity to be found in one of the protected workspaces in the US, this is in line with recent research from Infoblox , which found that residential proxies were widespread throughout enterprises. While not illegal per se, residential proxies can be used by bad actors for activities that most definitely are illicit, for example, denial-of-service operations or distribution of malware. The Residential Proxy Observatory has also found evidence of their activity on the island of St Helena, one of the most remote locations on the planet, so there really is no place on earth to hide from internet interference. This article first appeared on CSO .

title: Meta does a U-turn on controversial new AI terms for businesses
summary: Meta has hit pause on new terms of service for its business customers that would have granted it the right to grab any content from their websites. Not only that, but it would also have shifted the blame for every error produced through faulty AI to its customers. The new terms of service were revealed on October 19 and initially due to take effect on October 30, though Meta later pushed the start date back to November 20. But that small delay wasn’t enough to calm customer pushback, and now Meta has posted a note on Facebook’s business help center saying that the update had now been paused indefinitely . Given the strength of feeling, Meta’s U-turn will not have come as a surprise. The terms would have been seen as far too onerous for customers, as well as exposing them to a legal minefield of the sort that UK regulators recently warned about . In a statement to Harvard’s Nieman Lab , the company said that “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.” Meta has had a troubled time recently. Two weeks ago, it was fined for illegal use of customers’ data and in May, the company laid off 8,000 employees . This article first appeared on CIO .

title: Enterprises must take blame for their AI agents’ mistakes, say regulators
summary: The UK’s digital watchdogs have warned enterprises that they can’t evade their legal responsibilities by blaming errors on AI agents that they have deployed. “By taking action on behalf of users, such as making purchases and communicating with businesses, these agents could transform how people use digital services, engage with markets and unlock wider innovation,” said the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF), a body comprising the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), and communications regulator Ofcom, in a joint statement . While the DRCF welcomed such uses it advised, “firms developing or deploying personal agents should think carefully about how consumers can understand when and how an agent acts on their behalf, how authority to act is given and how their personal data is used.” The DRCF didn’t pull its punches. “We want to be explicit that existing legal and regulatory frameworks apply to personal AI agents, including competition, consumer and data protection law, online safety, financial services, payments and cyber security requirements,” it said, adding, “An AI agent’s autonomy does not diminish the responsibility of organisations that deploy it to comply with applicable law and relevant regulation.” There is certainly a degree of uncertainty over the legal position of autonomous AI agents. Gartner has warned that companies are increasingly facing legal challenges over “AI-induced” decisions, while attorneys have weighed in over gray areas in AI governance . The four UK regulators aren’t immune to that doubt: Only a few weeks earlier, they issued a Call for Input on their 2027-27 work plan to help them avoid overlap and uncertainty about the interplay between their respective regulatory regimes. This article first appeared on CIO .

title: OpenAI buys tiny software developer to improve Codex
summary: OpenAI is buying Pierre Computer Company in order to incorporate the San Francisco-based software developer’s Code.Storage infrastructure layer for Git into its Codex AI-powered programming tool. Pierre Computer, whose employees number just barely in the double digits, has got plenty of clout for its small size. It’s well-known for Code.Storage offering, as well as for its open-source software libraries, Trees and Diffs, which OpenAI already uses in Codex. OpenAI has experienced some of the limitations of Git itself, and its in-house engineering teams are already working to improve its support for human coders and AI agents working in parallel. Earlier this week the company described how it built a new back end for Git repositories , Pando, to enable concurrent working at scale. The AI developer has been pushing Codex more aggressively this year: offering it to Mac users and expanding it to Windows . It cited Pierre Computer’s ability to help developers review code as one of the reasons for the acquisition. OpenAI highlighted the Diffs’ Edit mode and the recently released Highlights as components that were particularly helpful to development teams. Announcing the deal on its news page, OpenAI set out how it would integrate the company into its existing offerings. “With the Pierre team, we wish to set the standard for modern software development: from the first branch an agent creates to that magic moment when code is deployed to the world. We want to make Codex the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects.” Neither company disclosed details of the acquisition price. OpenAI said that Code.Storage customers will be able to continue using the product until it brings the features into Codex, while Pierre Computer’s open-source projects will remain open, and OpenAI will continue to contribute to them. This article first appeared on InfoWorld .

title: Box launches Architect, an AI-powered workflow builder
summary: Box has introduced a new natural-language AI tool that helps users build automated workflows around document-related processes. Box Architect, announced at BoxWorks 2026 on Thursday, “effectively acts as an agentic operator of Box’s core content and workflow capabilities … to help customers design any content agentic workflow in Box,” said Aaron Levie, Box CEO, on X. To create a workflow, users describe in plain language a goal or process that they want to automate. Architect then defines the necessary stages and decisions, applying existing permissions, classifications, and retention policies related to content in Box. Users can test the workflow before it’s published, with options to insert requirements for human review and approvals. Once deployed, Architect can monitor a workflow’s outputs and recommend improvements as it’s continuously used. Architect interacts with multiple existing Box tools. A bank might use Architect to design and build a client onboarding workflow that collects applications via Box Forms, for example, then verify the documents with Box Extract, sign agreements with Box Sign, and begin account setup with Box Automate. Jason Andersen, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said Architect will make it easier to build agents and workflows based on the collective knowledge of a team or business, rather than focused only on their own productivity. As with any AI system that involves business data, customers will still need to evaluate how those workflows perform, said Andersen. “I’d still recommend human oversight during the creation process with any agent development project and using observability tools to make sure that the agents are running in a fashion that meets the risk and cost management needs of the business,” he said. title: Don’t mention the data center: OpenAI calls them ‘compute campuses’ instead
summary: OpenAI has responded to the data center culture war pitting communities against tech companies with a proposal to reduce its power demand during periods of grid strain. The company is also mindful of the bad publicity generated by talk of data centers and has renamed them “compute campuses” in an attempt to make them less scary. This is in line with the recent trend for renaming places like the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, or rebranding artificial intelligence as super intelligence . The new name cropped up four times, and data centers just twice, in OpenAI’s announcement of its Grid Protectors Program , a proposal to dial back electricity consumption in its data centers when demand is high so that nearby homes can continue to run their air conditioning or heating. Data centers’ increasing power consumption is straining the grid , with AI servers accounting for an ever larger share of that consumption, with further increases forecast . These demands are leading to a growing number of protests against the development of data centers , which could lead to construction delays. OpenAI claims that its Grid Protectors Program will meet some of those issues head-on by taking into account future capacity needs and working to make power flexibility a key element in data center, sorry, compute campus, design. The company said that the approach would differ, region by region. It has yet to finalize all the details of the scheme, but it hopes to head off some of the protests. It remains to be seen whether it has this effect. Google recently took the opposite approach to the peak consumption problem, proposing to pay people to turn off their appliances at times of high demand so that it can continue to power its data centers. This article first appeared on Network World .

summary: Remember when Google’s motto was “Don’t be evil”? Boy, wasn’t that a long time ago! It was more than ten years ago, and they replaced it in 2015 with “Do the right thing.” That hasn’t aged well either. Today, we’re seeing how Google’s losing-its-way is finally catching up with the onetime darling of the no-longer-quite-so-magnificent Magnificent Seven . There are many reasons why big tech players are floundering in shrinking valuations AI infrastructure overspending and the political backlash against AI data centers . But Google, Google is special. title: Google Pics: How to level up your visuals in Docs and Slides
summary: Simplicity and convenience are a tough combo to beat. That’s why basic features integrated into the productivity apps we’re already using almost always win out over more capable and complex third-party options, at least when it comes to most mainstream use — and why Google’s latest easily overlooked addition to its Workspace office suite is well worth your while to notice. The addition is called, rather confusingly, Google Pics. (If you ever mix up Google Pics with Google Photos or Google Images, don’t worry: Google Lens can help you sort it out.) Pics, unlike its similarly named Google app contemporaries, is meant to exist primarily within the Google Drive ecosystem as opposed to being its own standalone entity. The easiest way to think about it is as a newly souped-up, superpowered image editor and graphic creator that lives directly within Google Docs and Slides — and, eventually, also within Drive itself. It’s a fuss-free way to let you make new artwork and refine existing images in your documents and presentations, and it’s surprisingly powerful and effective in what it’s able to do. Critically, it’s also both simple and convenient, as an option within any document or deck you’re already working on. All you’ve gotta do is (a) realize it’s there and available to you and (b) learn how to best take advantage of the new powers it affords you. Here’s your start-to-finish guide. Provided you fit the bill, just open up Docs or Slides like you normally would, then click on any image within your document or presentation and look for the “Edit” option beneath it. title: Everything you need to know about the new MacBook Pro’s OLED display
summary: Apple’s recently introduced MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR introduces a tandem OLED display and, for the first time, a touch interface. I discussed the approach Apple took to designing its new pro laptop with Apple’s Vice President of Mac and iPad Product Marketing, Tom Boger, which you can read here . What follows is a little more information on some of the product features people are asking about, along with my first impressions of interacting with the display. How the panel is made The PROLED XDR display is made of 50 layers that total less than one millimeter. It’s a single sheet of glass carrying more than 100 million thin film transistors, arranged in 15 layers under 10 microns thick. The tandem OLED layers sit on top of this: two stacks making up 30 layers, each between a few nanometers and a few hundred nanometers thick. Apple wanted to make the display as thin as possible, because a thin display delivers much better performance and the company wanted to optimize the OLED technology. Apple took great pains in building this; it even worked with its display supplier to simulate how OLED molecules evaporate onto the glass and to track each layer’s thickness as it comes off the line. It was interesting to learn that the panels are made on giant sheets of “mother glass,” with about eighty 14-inch panels per sheet. The final layers add mechanical, electrical and thermal benefits, with optical adhesive and a cover glass with anti-reflective and fingerprint-resistant coatings placed on top. One industry observer I spoke with remarked that these high-end display fabrication factories are massive, the size of football stadiums, with the most extreme needs for clean-room suits and high-tech protection. What this means for the display The up to 2,000 nits display delivers stunning clarity with a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The Democratic sweep intensified fears over runaway spending, mounting debt and resistance to datacentres, sending tech shares tumbling. title: Enterprises must take blame for their AI agents’ mistakes, say regulators
summary: The UK’s digital watchdogs have warned enterprises that they can’t evade their legal responsibilities by blaming errors on AI agents that they have deployed. “By taking action on behalf of users, such as making purchases and communicating with businesses, these agents could transform how people use digital services, engage with markets and unlock wider innovation,” said the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF), a body comprising the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), and communications regulator Ofcom, in a joint statement . While the DRCF welcomed such uses it advised, “firms developing or deploying personal agents should think carefully about how consumers can understand when and how an agent acts on their behalf, how authority to act is given and how their personal data is used.” The DRCF didn’t pull its punches. “We want to be explicit that existing legal and regulatory frameworks apply to personal AI agents, including competition, consumer and data protection law, online safety, financial services, payments and cyber security requirements,” it said, adding, “An AI agent’s autonomy does not diminish the responsibility of organisations that deploy it to comply with applicable law and relevant regulation.” There is certainly a degree of uncertainty over the legal position of autonomous AI agents. Gartner has warned that companies are increasingly facing legal challenges over “AI-induced” decisions, while attorneys have weighed in over gray areas in AI governance . The four UK regulators aren’t immune to that doubt: Only a few weeks earlier, they issued a Call for Input on their 2027-27 work plan to help them avoid overlap and uncertainty about the interplay between their respective regulatory regimes. This article first appeared on CIO .

The attack could expose AI hosting providers that allow customers to upload and run their own models, potentially giving attackers a foothold inside infrastructure processing requests for multiple customers, the post added. However, the Python Security Response Team (PSRT), which handles security reports involving CPython, disputed the security implications of the demonstration in a response to CSO. “We acknowledge the underlying CPython bug reported by RunSybil and appreciate their contribution to fixing it. However, we do not consider the demonstrated sandbox escape to be a CPython security vulnerability,” the team said. The disagreement centres on whether the interpreter should be responsible for preventing sandbox escapes. While RunSybil argues that the flaw creates risks for AI inference infrastructure, PSRT says executing untrusted Python code within a sandbox is outside CPython’s security threat model. title: Why edge-cloud AI inference pipelines are key
summary: Most enterprise AI conversations still start in the wrong place. They begin with models, platforms, and cloud services. Which foundation model is best? Which provider has the most GPUs ? Which tool can build the flashiest demo? Those questions matter, but they are not where production AI usually succeeds or fails. The better question is: Where should the inference actually happen? That sounds simple, but it is becoming one of the most important architecture decisions in AI. Not all inference belongs in the central cloud. Not all inference belongs on the device. Not all inference belongs at the edge . The right answer usually involves all three, working together as a pipeline. I call this an edge-cloud AI inference architecture. It splits AI workloads across devices, edge locations, and centralized cloud platforms so latency-sensitive decisions happen close to the user or machine, while heavier reasoning, aggregation, governance, and retraining remain centralized. This is where the next generation of useful enterprise AI systems is headed. Latency changes the design Cloud-first AI works well when the user can wait. A chatbot can tolerate a few hundred milliseconds, sometimes more. A document analysis workflow can wait seconds. A batch analytics process can wait minutes or hours. Many operational AI systems cannot. A manufacturing robot cannot wait for a round trip to a distant cloud region before stopping a defective process. A retail checkout camera cannot depend on a remote model call for every frame. A vehicle, medical device, warehouse scanner, or energy-grid controller cannot treat network latency as an afterthought. In these cases, inference needs to happen locally or very close to the source. That may mean on the device itself, on an on-premises edge server, in a telecom edge facility, or in a regional micro data center. The point is not the label. The point is proximity. title: Windows 11 is 40% faster on computers with 8GB of RAM
summary: Microsoft has implemented several optimizations designed to make Windows 11 significantly faster on computers with as little as 8GB of RAM. According to the company’s own tests, responsiveness has already improved by up to 20% , while multitasking is now up to 40% faster. To achieve this, Microsoft has developed a more efficient memory compression technique that allows up to 2GB of active data to remain in RAM instead of being moved to slower storage. Microsoft has also optimized features such as the Start menu, the search function, Settings, and File Explorer. These are now up to 20% faster compared to January 2026, the company said in a blog post . Microsoft’s own applications have also been improved. Edge can now launch up to 33% faster, while Teams can open up to 20% faster. At the same time, memory usage in Windows, Edge, and Microsoft 365 has been reduced by up to 900MB. The improvements in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook alone account for about 360MB in savings. To take advantage of these improvements, you need Windows 11 version 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later. Some improvements also require updating Microsoft’s apps. This article originally appeared on Computer Sweden .
